name: North Baker and Boldt Hall Courtyard
Boldt Hall Arch
funFact: Boldt Tower features an embedded red sandstone block taken from the original Waldorf Astoria hotel in Manhattan, given that the complex was named in honor of Cornell trustee and hotel proprietor George C. Boldt.

name: Baker Laboratory 200
funFact:
1. More than 40 percent of all Cornell students will sit in Baker 200 at some point during their undergraduate career.
2. The Nobel Prize Predictor: The room hosts the famous Baker Lectures - the oldest continuous chemistry lecture series in the United States (established in 1923). Amazingly, 21 Baker Lecturers have gone on to win the Nobel Prize, meaning a presentation in this hall is historically one of the strongest indicators of future Nobel glory.

name: Goldwin Smith 132
funFact: Goldwin Smith 132 has a reputation for having some of the most sensitive row desks on campus. Because of how the long wooden desks are anchored, if a single student at the end of a row shakes their leg or erases a mistake aggressively, the entire row vibrates like a mini-earthquake, rattling the laptops and notebooks of everyone sitting in it.

name: Cornell Health 1st Floor
funFact: Prescribing... Mother Nature? Cornell Health was a pioneer in creating Nature Rx @Cornell, a program where clinicians literally write "prescriptions" for stressed-out students to spend time in the campus's famous gorges and botanical gardens to lower their cortisol levels

name: Willard Straight 414
funFact: This room features a stunning series of historic paintings displayed on its walls. These were personally collected by Willard Straight himself during his late 19th and early 20th-century travels through East Asia while working as a U.S. diplomat and financial emissary

name: Willard Straight 6th Floor
funFact: Rooms 604 and 605 are officially designated as Loft 1 and Loft 2. They serve as cozy, high-demand meeting spots for student club executive boards. Because they feature slanted ceilings and high stone-framed windows directly under the building’s peaks, it feels like holding a club meeting inside a medieval fortress.

name: Willard Straight Rock Garden
funFact: The garden lines the banks of a small, waterfall-filled stream known across campus by its official, highly unglamorous nickname: Wee Stinky Creek. The name dates back to the early 20th century when the College of Veterinary Science was located nearby and literally drained operational chemicals and animal waste directly into the stream, creating a notorious campus stench. While the creek has been completely clean for decades, the funny historical name permanently stuck

name: A.D. White Gardens
funFact: Located behind the A.D. White House, the garden owes its existence to an incredibly formidable woman. The garden was first cultivated by A.D. White’s second wife, Helen Magill White, who made history as the very first woman in the United States to earn a Ph.D (in Greek from Boston University).

name: The Secret Garden
funFact: The A.D. White House Secret Garden is a beautifully preserved Victorian-style green space that blends natural serenity with Cornell history. The grand carriage house that sits right next to the secret garden was later converted into what students now know as the Big Red Barn.

name: West Campus Underground Tunnel System
funFact: While the new residential halls have clean, well-lit corridors for students, a separate, highly dangerous network of historic 1920s steam tunnels runs under the Gothic section of West Campus.

name: Barton Hall
funFact: Built between 1914 and 1917 as a military drill hall, Barton Hall's massive open layout allowed it to function as a hangar and ground school for military aeronautics during World War I.

name: Uris G01
funFact: Uris G01 features a monochromatic, aggressively bright red design spanning from the floor carpets to the seats and walls. Maybe the unrelenting red walls are widely joked to be a form of psychological warfare, intentionally amplifying test-taking anxiety right before a major prelim or final exam

name: Ezra Cornell's Tomb Inside Sage Chapel Crypt
funFact: Did you know Ezra Cornell himself rests inside a secure stone crypt sealed beneath a 700-pound slab of stone in Sage Chapel, while a life-sized marble statue of him lies directly above it to guard his true resting place?

name: Underground Tunnel From Barton Hall
funFact: Did you know there exists a lengthy underground tunnel from Barton Hall?

name: The Swinging Bench
funFact: "It don't mean a thing, if it ain't got that swing!" - Duke Ellington.

name: Sage Hall
funFact: Sage Hall actually opened in 1875 as Cornell’s first residential building for female students. At the time, it was considered one of the most luxurious college dormitories in the United States!

name: Lincoln Hall Neylan Rehearsal Hall
funFact: Lincoln Hall was originally built in 1888 with an entirely flat back facade because the university ran out of money to finish its planned east wing mid-construction. For over a century, civil engineering students - and later, music students - had to use a structurally lopsided building until a massive $19 million expansion in 2000 finally completed the architects' original vision 112 years later.

name: Path from Sage Hall to Ho Plaza
The Terrace Kitchen
funFact: The name "terrace" is deeply rooted in Cornell history, founders Ezra Cornell and Andrew Dickson White originally envisioned the entire campus layout as a "grand terrace" overlooking Ithaca and Cayuga Lake

name: The Ramin Room
funFact: The room honors Richard M. Ramin ('51), a legendary varsity football player who transitioned into a powerhouse Cornell administrator, serving the university for 41 years!

name: Statler Hall Auditorium
funFact: Statler Hall's Nolan School of Hotel Administration gets a famous shout-out in the 1987 film Dirty Dancing. The owner of Kellerman’s resort proudly boasts that his grandson, Neil, attends the "Cornell School of Hotel Administration."

name: Mann Library Gallery
funFact: While the original Art Deco library building itself opened in the early 1950s, the second-floor gallery was added in 2007 during a massive modernization project that also introduced the library's five-story central atrium.

name: Barton Hall Tower Staircase
funFact: Before Barton Hall's towers went up, the site was home to Cornell's third astronomical observatory, which had to be demolished to make room for the drill hall.

name: The Libe Slope
funFact: "Libe" is simply short for "Library," referring to Uris Library sitting right at the crest of the hill. Students have used the slang term for over a hundred years. It appeared in The Cornell Daily Sun as early as 1926 in a joke about building a fence to block the brutal Ithaca wind.

name: Milstein Hall
funFact: Milstein Hall is cooled using cold water pumped from the bottom of Cayuga Lake, and its interior features a giant concrete dome that pulls double duty as both a ceiling and stadium seating.

name: Green Dragon Café
funFact: The Green Dragon Café’s iconic ceiling is actually made out of repurposed empty tin cans from Cornell Dining. When architecture, art, and planning students built the café in 1968 using a $100 advance from the college dean, they designed the ceiling with hundreds of salvaged tin cans to house minimalist lighting and give the basement space a cozy, eclectic vibe.

name: Rhodes-Rawlings Auditorium, Klarman G70
funFact: Alumni Judith Lund Biggs '57 and Suzanne Weiss funded the naming of the auditorium to honor both Rhodes (Cornell's 9th president) and Rawlings (Cornell's 10th president).

name: Abby and Howard Milstein Auditorium
funFact: The auditorium's tiered seating is literally built on the outside slope of a giant concrete dome. The inside of that same dome forms a separate, cavern-like critique and exhibition space underneath the auditorium.

name: Beebe Lake Trail
funFact: Beebe Lake is completely man-made and used to feature a giant toboggan slide that launched riders onto the frozen water. Before university founder Ezra Cornell built a dam across Fall Creek in 1838 to power local mills, the entire area along the trail was just a tangled, forested swamp.
